scenes.visual: Continue the first film's dark 16:9 world without resetting the colour map: exons BLUE, introns RED, cap and tail GOLD, recognition signals and active splice choices TEAL. The finished capped and tailed message from the first film fills 65% of the width. Its BLUE joins pulse, then a fresh schematic pre-mRNA copy with RED introns appears beside it, labelled 'another copy of the same gene's transcript'. A protein-reading strip appears below with a question mark. Keep a small 'schematic' label visible.
Title 'When the Joins Change' fades in above the carried transcript for two seconds. The BLUE blocks drift gently while two TEAL possible join arcs shimmer.

scenes.tts: Splicing need not make one pattern. A cell may skip an exon, shift a splice site, choose between exons, or retain an intron. Each choice makes a different messenger RNA. Regulatory signals can make these patterns differ among tissues.

scenes.visual: Keep one large pre-mRNA centered and label it 'one of many copies'. Transform it through the common patterns instead of cutting to a list; each transformation stands for a different copy, not a re-splicing of one molecule. One BLUE block lifts out for 'skip'; a TEAL boundary slides for 'shift'; two BLUE alternatives trade places; then one RED ribbon stays between BLUE blocks. A small stack of finished messages grows at the right, one per transformation.

scenes.tts: A sequence change can weaken a normal splice site. Nearby sites then compete differently. A weakened splice site most often causes exon skipping. Less often, a cryptic site takes over or the intron is retained. One allele can make several products at once.

scenes.visual: Return to one junction. Its TEAL normal-site flag dims but is not crossed out. Two smaller TEAL flags nearby brighten, each labelled 'possible cryptic site'. Join arcs compete with slow pulses. The RNA then branches into three schematic products: a wide lane labelled 'skip (most often)', and two narrower lanes labelled 'cryptic site' and 'retain'. Lane widths are schematic, with no numeric ratio.

scenes.tts: One studied beta thalassemia allele made two abnormal RNAs in cultured cells. The main product kept part of an intron. A smaller amount joined nonadjacent exons. One changed splice signal shifted competition in more than one way.

The narrower lane joins the first BLUE exon directly to a later BLUE exon. Lane widths convey 'main' and 'smaller amount' schematically, without a numeric ratio.

scenes.tts: Length is only the first consequence. In coding sequence, ribosomes read bases in groups called codons. Changing the length can shift every downstream group, changing many amino acids. A shift after one junction can change every later codon boundary.

scenes.visual: A BLUE coding message stretches across the frame. Under it, a computed triplet ruler groups letter placeholders into repeating boxes. The groups glide left to right as a reading marker advances. Then a middle BLUE exon lifts slightly; all downstream boxes glow GOLD to show they could be affected. No protein structure is drawn.

scenes.tts: This outlined exon contains only complete codon groups. Imagine that splicing skips it. Use the ruler, not the exon count. Will the downstream groups stay aligned, or will every boundary move?

scenes.visual: Highlight one invented BLUE exon with a bright WHITE outline (outside the colour map). It contains four complete triplet boxes and is labelled on screen '12 coding nucleotides'; this computed example differs from the lesson's worked values. The exon hovers above a gap. Large question text appears: 'Do downstream triplets stay aligned?'
Deliberate thinking pause. Hold the lifted WHITE-outlined exon, the gap, and the question. The reading marker bobs gently and the downstream triplet boundaries shimmer without moving.

scenes.tts: They stay aligned. Removing complete codon groups changes the message's length but not its downstream grouping. Whole triplets leave, so the next base begins a codon normally. The new junction can still matter, because sequence determines what it encodes.

scenes.visual: Clear the question. The WHITE-outlined exon leaves, and the flanking BLUE blocks slide together. The downstream triplet ruler keeps every boundary fixed relative to the reading marker. A green 'aligned' bracket appears. Then the new junction pulses with a question mark labelled 'sequence still matters'.

scenes.tts: Now skip a coding segment with one extra base beyond complete groups. Every downstream boundary shifts. The reading marker now meets different base groups. A premature stop becomes likely, although only the sequence can show where one appears.

Highlight a different invented exon with a WHITE outline, labelled on screen '10 coding nucleotides': three full triplet boxes plus one WHITE-outlined leftover base. When it lifts out, slide every downstream triplet boundary by one position. A stop-shaped marker with a question mark drifts along the downstream region; do not place a definite stop.

scenes.tts: The remainder test applies to net changes inside coding sequence. It does not predict effects of untranslated changes. It also cannot tell whether an RNA is exported, degraded, or translated. Those fates require evidence beyond a length calculation.

scenes.visual: The transcript receives brackets for 'untranslated' at both ends and 'coding sequence' in the middle. The triplet ruler remains only under the coding bracket. Three neutral question tags appear beside the finished RNA: 'export?', 'decay?', and 'translation?'. They remain unanswered, matching the narration's limit.

scenes.tts: Processing still marks transcript ends and chooses which segments join into messenger RNA. For coding consequences, keep a second rule. Coding length changes keep the downstream frame only in multiples of three. It applies only when the changed nucleotides are coding. Sequence decides the actual protein outcome. That is the scope of this rule.
